clinicalPearls: Characterised by a marfanoid habitus combined with craniosynostosis and, in most cases, intellectual disability, which helps distinguish it from Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes
Caused by pathogenic variants in SKI, usually arising de novo, affecting a regulator of transforming growth factor beta signalling
Craniofacial features include craniosynostosis, dolichocephaly, hypertelorism, proptosis, a high-arched palate and micrognathia
Skeletal features overlap with Marfan syndrome: arachnodactyly, dolichostenomelia, pectus deformity, scoliosis and joint hypermobility or contractures
Hypotonia, developmental delay and intellectual disability are common and are more prominent than in other marfanoid connective-tissue disorders
Aortic root dilatation can occur but is generally milder and less frequent than in Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndromes, so cardiovascular surveillance is still warranted
Additional features include hernias and, in some, brain anomalies such as Chiari I malformation
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic pattern of findings with confirmatory SKI genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome is a heritable connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in SKI, which encodes a repressor of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) signalling. Loss of normal SKI-mediated repression is thought to enhance TGF-beta signalling, a mechanism shared with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, disturbing the development and integrity of connective tissue, bone and the cardiovascular system. This produces the marfanoid skeletal habitus, the craniofacial features including premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis), and connective-tissue laxity, alongside the neurodevelopmental impairment that distinguishes the condition. Aortic root involvement reflects the same connective-tissue vulnerability but tends to be less severe than in related aortopathies.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey for scoliosis, pectus and limb proportions
Brain MRI when Chiari malformation or other anomaly is suspected
redFlags: Airway or feeding difficulties from craniofacial anomalies
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of skeletal, neurological and cardiovascular involvement; intellectual disability is common, and although aortic disease is usually milder than in Marfan syndrome, cardiovascular surveillance remains important.
pitfalls: Labelling the patient as having Marfan syndrome and missing the craniosynostosis and intellectual disability
Assuming aortic involvement is absent and omitting cardiovascular surveillance
Overlooking raised intracranial pressure from suture fusion
Attributing developmental delay to an unrelated cause

management: Cardiovascular surveillance with serial echocardiography for aortic root dilatation, with beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker therapy to reduce aortic wall stress when dilatation is present
Prophylactic aortic root surgery if dilatation progresses to established surgical criteria
Craniofacial and neurosurgical assessment of craniosynostosis with cranial vault expansion where raised intracranial pressure or progressive deformity demands it
Orthopaedic management of scoliosis, pectus deformity and joint hypermobility or contractures with bracing, physiotherapy or corrective surgery
Early developmental intervention and educational support for hypotonia, developmental delay and intellectual disability, with ophthalmological review
Coordinated multidisciplinary care across clinical genetics, cardiology, craniofacial surgery, orthopaedics and developmental paediatrics
Genetic counselling explaining the usually de novo SKI variant and consequently low recurrence risk
